chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Musa ibn Sa'dan from al-Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala' from Isma'il ibn 'Ammar from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who has a loan with another man, so he gives him something from the profit, fearing that he might cut that off from him, so he takes his money, without it being a condition upon him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no harm with it, as long as it was not a condition.'
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar said: I wrote to the latter (Imam al-Hadi or al-Hasan al-Askari, peace be upon him)

A man has a hundred dirhams due from another man, so he binds him to it and says to him: 'Return to me in ten days and I will pay your debt.' If I do not return, then a thousand dirhams are due from me, payable immediately, without a condition, and I bear witness to that upon him. Then he called them to witness, and the Imam (peace be upon him) ruled: 'It is not fitting for them to witness except with the truth, and it is not fitting for the creditor to take except the truth, if God wills.'
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to give a debtor a gift to ensure repayment without it being considered a condition of the loan?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the distinction between a voluntary gift (hibah) given to encourage repayment and a formal conditional penalty (shart), establishing that extra payments are permissible only if not contractually bound. The second report highlights the scholarly principle that creditors may only claim what is truly owed unless a specific condition was agreed upon, reinforcing the Shia emphasis on fairness and avoiding unjust enrichment in debt transactions. This ruling underscores the importance of distinguishing between customary practice and legal obligation in Islamic commercial jurisprudence.
